Triggers.value: A specific temperature on the skin
A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Paying attention to or looking at my own body
Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
Any form of physical contact with others

Threat.value: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly

Negative Appraisals.value: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next
I am permanently an outsider now

issues.item: Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
issues.explanation: The social avoidance items are difficult to reconcile with the stated trauma type of childhood physical abuse by a caregiver. These triggers imply avoidance of people linked to a discrete later-life event, but the trauma is chronic/developmental and caregiver-based; there is no corresponding trigger or appraisal content tying prior social contacts or specific intimacy-linked reminders to the abuse history.

issues.item: Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others
issues.explanation: Intrusion Monitoring suggests fear of an intruder entering the home, which fits home-invasion or stalking trauma better than childhood caregiver physical abuse. With no accompanying memory or trigger content about nighttime entry, footsteps, doors, or home intrusion, this threat item is hard to explain from the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: No Good Ahead and Outsider are broad, depressive or social-identity appraisals, whereas the other active content is dominated by vigilance, bodily threat detection, and sensory triggering. This combination is not impossible, but here the intimacy/social avoidance items appear to depend on relational shame or alienation that is otherwise underdeveloped and weakly connected to the trigger/threat pattern, reducing coherence.

issues.item: No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore
issues.explanation: Given the formulation, Triggers and Negative Appraisals should be tightly linked, but the chosen triggers are mainly tactile/somatic/intrusive-memory cues while two maladaptive strategies focus on avoiding social contacts and intimacy. Those strategies are not well supported by the trigger set and feel targeted at a different symptom cluster than the one represented elsewhere.

vignette: When James first stepped onto the floor of the cramped apartment that he now shared with his wife, the cold ceramic tiles under his feet felt as if they were biting. The night of the incident, the same floor had been a battlefield: his mother, who had long withheld affection, had taken a wooden spoon from the kitchen and slammed it against his chest until his breath caught. The shock that followed had been as sharp as the spoon, and the memory of that slamming sound still rises to the surface whenever he feels a sudden chill on his skin. His own heart starts to pound at the slightest draft of air, and he finds himself staring at the wall in a panic, as if the threat could reappear from the corners of the room. The tactile trigger of temperature-whether a cool breeze on a summer evening or the warmth of a hand-has become a constant alarm. Each time James feels a slight change in his skin's temperature, he automatically scans for danger, as if the world were suddenly rearmed with weapons. The recognition of potential weapons-metal desks, the office computer tower, even a child's toy on the floor-feeds into his sense of threat. When his body reacts before his mind has a chance to process, a surge of adrenaline takes over, forcing him to freeze or bolt. That startle response to touch-when a coworker reaches out to pass a file, when a colleague pats his shoulder in greeting-makes his chest tighten and his breath come shallow, as though his body had been trained to anticipate violence long before the mind can react. These physical sensations do more than just frighten him; they reinforce his negative beliefs about the world. The constant vigilance he has developed leads him to believe that danger lurks around every corner, that people are unreliable, and that he is forever an outsider. The memory of the spoon's impact convinces him that no one can be trusted. In return, these appraisals heighten his triggers: the simple feeling of a cool breeze now feels like a prelude to attack, and any sudden, unexpected touch is interpreted as a threat. The sense of threat, in turn, brings the triggers back into focus, creating a self-reinforcing loop. When the threat of potential danger looms, James's body responds with heat, and his heart races, which then confirms his belief that the world is unsafe. Likewise, the belief that he is permanently an outsider fuels his avoidance of any situation where he might have to look at his own body. He no longer watches his posture or his hands; instead, he keeps his eyes down or looks away whenever he notices his own reflection, fearing that his own body might be the next target. He also keeps his distance from colleagues at work, preferring to work in silence, his keyboard his only companion. When a coworker asks him to join a project meeting, he declines, fearing the possibility of unexpected physical contact or the social scrutiny that might reveal his vulnerability. Each time he refuses to engage, his mistrust of people is reinforced, and his perception of threat grows. His avoidance of social contact and of being touched have taken on concrete occupational consequences. In the open-plan office where his software team collaborates, James sits alone at a quiet corner, surrounded by stacks of code. The fluorescent lights flicker and, at times, he experiences the same racing heartbeat that once accompanied the memory of a spoon. His avoidance of the break room-where colleagues gather around the coffee machine-means he misses out on the small rituals that strengthen his team's cohesion. The avoidance of his own body has manifested in his reluctance to accept physical feedback from his supervisor, who often pats his back when a task is completed. James now reports that even the sight of a colleague's friendly smile feels threatening; he interprets it as a potential weapon in disguise, because he cannot trust that it will not turn hostile. The cycle that began with a spoon on a cold night now permeates James's daily life, and he feels trapped. He has gone months feeling a chill, racing heart, and a sudden recollection of that night whenever he hears the buzz of a computer or the hiss of a refrigerator. The belief that he is forever an outsider has made him believe that there is no place for him in the world, no safe harbor. This conviction fuels his avoidance of touch and of people, which in turn keeps him isolated. His body continues to react before he can process, and his mind is locked in a loop of threat anticipation. The pattern has intensified over the years, leaving James exhausted, paranoid, and increasingly lonely. It is only after a particularly harrowing episode-when he nearly fell over a spilled cup of coffee on his desk, his heart pounding and his mind racing that a hidden danger was imminent-that he reached out for help. He fears that if he does not find a way to break this cycle, he will lose his job, his relationship, and perhaps even his sense of self. What he most hopes for is a way to quiet the alarm in his body, to feel safe enough to look at his own reflection, and to trust that the people around him are not weapons waiting to strike.
